title: Phonics & Reading
description: From hearing sounds in words to fluent, thoughtful reading. Systematic synthetic phonics in the early stages (sounds → blending → decodable words), then fluency, comprehension strategies, and finally critical reading of complex texts.

goals: Hear the first sound in a spoken word
Link the sounds s, a, t, p, i, n to their letters

lessons.title: What Sound Does It Start With?
objectives: Hear the first sound in a spoken word
Find objects that start with the same sound
prerequisites: Can listen to and repeat short words
explanation: Every word we say is made of sounds. "Sun" starts with a hissing snake sound: sss. "Mango" starts with a humming sound: mmm.
We are listening for the SOUND, not the letter name. The sound of s is "sss", not "ess". Stretch the start of a word to hear it: "sssun".
Words can share a first sound: sun, sock and sandwich all start with sss. Playing "I spy something beginning with mmm" trains your listening ears.

vocabulary.meaning: what we hear when we say part of a word
the sound at the very start of a word
words that end with the same sound, like cat and hat

examples: Ball, bat and bus all start with b.
Moon and mango start with mmm; sun does not.

story.title: Olu's Sound Basket
story.text: Olu the owl had a basket for things starting with sss. Kiko brought a sock — in it went! Then a spoon — in it went! Then Kiko brought a banana. "Bbb-banana," Olu listened. "That starts with bbb, not sss. It needs the b-basket!" Kiko laughed and made a second basket.

activities.prompt: Which starts with the same sound as SUN ☀️?
Which starts with mmm?
Match the pictures that start with the same sound
Cat and cup start with the same sound.

thinking: Does your name start with the same sound as anyone else's in your family?
Why do you think we stretch the first sound when we listen?
speaking: Play I-spy with a grown-up using sounds: "I spy something beginning with…" and explain your clue.

project.title: Sound Treasure Hunt

Hunt for 5 things that start with that sound

Put a wrong one in the basket and see if a grown-up can find it

assessment.prompt: Ball and bat start with the same sound.

mastery: Identifies the first sound in spoken words reliably
Sorts objects or pictures by first sound
Produces a word with a given first sound

lessons.title: Letters Make Sounds
objectives: Say the sound (not the name) for each letter a to z
Blend two sounds into a word: a-t → at, i-n → in, u-p → up
prerequisites: Can hear the first sound in a word
explanation: Letters are shapes that stand for sounds. We say the SOUND, not the letter name: s says "sss" like a snake, m says "mmm" like yummy food, a says "a" as in apple.
Short sounds like b, d, g, p and t are said quickly and cleanly, with no "uh" after them: "b", not "buh". This makes blending much easier later.
Blending means pushing sounds together to make a word. Start with just two sounds: a… t… a-t… at! i… n… in! u… p… up! This is exactly how IVU Reads starts too (Levels 0 and 1).

vocabulary.meaning: a written shape for a sound
what the letter says, like "sss" for s
push sounds together to say a word
touching under each letter as you say its sound

examples: a-t blends to at; i-n blends to in.
u-p blends to up; o-n blends to on.

story.title: The Little Red Car
story.text: Ivaan's little red car drove along a road of letters. At the a it said "a!", and at the t it said "t!" Then it drove faster and faster — a-t, a-t — until the two sounds bumped together: "at!" "I made a word!" Ivaan cheered. The car beeped and drove off to find i and n.

activities.prompt: Blend: a – t
Blend: u – p
Match the letter to its picture
Which is the sound of s?

thinking: Why do we say "sss" and not "ess" when we read?
Can you think of a word that starts with the sound "mmm"?
speaking: Read "at", "in" and "up" to a grown-up by touching each letter as you say its sound, then saying the whole word.

project.title: Sandy Letters
steps: Look at a letter card and say its sound

mastery: Says the sound for each letter on sight (IVU Reads Level 0)
Says b, d, g, p, t without adding "uh"

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: The Vowel in the Middle
objectives: Read 3-letter words with all five short vowels
Segment spoken 3-letter words into three sounds
prerequisites: Knows the letter sounds and reads 2-letter words
explanation: Many short words are like a sandwich: a consonant, a vowel in the middle, and a consonant — like c-a-t or d-o-g. We call them CVC words.

The five vowels a, e, i, o, u are the "filling". Learn them in order: short a (cat, map, van), then short i and o (pig, dog, hot), then short u and e (sun, bus, bed, hen) — the same order as IVU Reads Levels 2, 3 and 4.
To read, say each sound and blend: c… a… t… cat! To spell, do the opposite: say the word slowly and write a letter for each sound you hear. That is called segmenting.

vocabulary.meaning: one of the letters a, e, i, o, u
any letter that is not a vowel
consonant, vowel, consonant, like cat
split a word into its sounds

examples: c-a-t → cat; p-i-g → pig; b-u-s → bus.
Changing the vowel: hat → hit → hot → hut.

story.title: The Magic Middle
story.text: Rangi the chameleon could change colour — and words! Rangi sat on the word "hat" and turned purple: it became "hit". Rangi turned blue: "hot". Then orange: "hut". "I only changed the middle sound," Rangi giggled, "but each time I made a new word!"

activities.prompt: Read: d – o – g
Match the word to the picture
Which word has the sound "e" in the middle?
Put the sounds in order to make "map"

thinking: How many new words can you make by changing only the middle sound of "hat"?
Why are vowels important in almost every word?
speaking: Read five 3-letter words to a grown-up, then explain how you worked out the hardest one.

project.title: Word Slider

project.safety: Use child-safe scissors with adult supervision. Adults should handle any sharp cutting tools and keep small pieces away from younger children.

mastery: Reads short a, i, o, u and e words accurately (IVU Reads Levels 2–4)

lessons.title: sh, ch, th and ck
objectives: Read words containing sh, ch, th and ck
Recognise that two letters can make one sound, and know the first star words
explanation: Sometimes two letters work together to make ONE sound. We call them a sound pair (or digraph). s and h together say "sh", like a quiet finger on your lips: ship, fish, shop.
c and h say "ch" like a train: chin, chip, chop. t and h say "th" — stick your tongue out a little: thin, bath, moth. c and k together say just "k": duck, sock, rock.
Star words (sight words) like "the", "said" and "was" don't follow the usual rules, so we learn them by heart. IVU Reads practises these in Levels 5 to 7.

vocabulary.meaning: two letters that make one sound
a dot under the letters for each sound
a word we learn by sight, like "the" or "said"

examples: sh: ship, fish, shop; ch: chin, chip.
th: thin, bath; ck: duck, sock, rock.

story.title: The Quiet Ship
story.text: A big ship sailed past the harbour. "SHHH!" said Momo the bear. "The baby fish are sleeping." Everyone whispered. "Sh is the sleeping sound," said Momo. When the fish woke up, a duck went quack and the little fish swam off — ch-ch-ch — like a train.

activities.prompt: Which word has "sh"?
How many SOUNDS in "fish"? f-i-sh 🔵🔵🔵
activities.why: sh is two letters but one sound.

activities.prompt: Match
In "chip", c and h make one sound together.

thinking: Why can't we just read "s" then "h" in ship? What would it sound like?
Why do you think some words are "star words" that we learn by heart?
speaking: Teach a grown-up the actions for sh (finger on lips), ch (train) and th (tongue out), and read one word for each.

lessons.title: I Can Read a Story!
objectives: Read 2- and 3-word phrases and short sentences
Read a short decodable story and answer a question about it
prerequisites: Reads 3-letter words, sound pairs and some star words
explanation: Once we can read words, we can read them together. Two words make a phrase: "big dog", "red car". Three words: "a red car", "the big dog".
A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop: "The cat sat on a mat." Point to each word with your finger as you read it.

A story is a few sentences in a row. After reading, a good reader can answer questions: Who? What? Where? IVU Reads practises this in Levels 8 to 12, with stories like "Ivu and the Red Car" and "The Mud Pig".

vocabulary.meaning: a small group of words, like "big dog"
words that make a complete thought, ending with a full stop
the big letter at the start of a sentence
the dot at the end of a sentence

examples: The cat sat on a mat.
Ivu has a red car.

story.title: Ivu and the Red Car
story.text: Ivu has a red car. The car is fast. Ivu gets in the car. Up the hill went the car! Then the car had to stop. Ivu hops off and has a hot bun.

activities.prompt: In the story, what colour is the car?
Put the words in order to make a sentence

A sentence ends with a full stop.

Why do we point to each word when we read?

lessons.title: The Split Digraph (Magic e)
objectives: Read words with split digraphs a-e, i-e, o-e, u-e
Explain how the final e changes the vowel sound
prerequisites: Reads CVC words and common digraphs
explanation: Look at "cap" and "cape". Adding e at the end changes the short "a" into a long "ay" sound. The a and the e work as a team even though a letter sits between them — a split digraph.
It works for other vowels: pin → pine, hop → hope, cub → cube. The e itself is silent; its job is to change the vowel.
Reading tip: when you see a vowel, one consonant, then e at the end, try the long vowel sound first.

vocabulary.meaning: two vowel letters split by a consonant that make one long sound
a vowel that says its name, like a in cake
a letter we write but do not say

examples: kit → kite, not → note.
tub → tube; man → mane.

story.title: The Sneaky e
story.text: Little e loved jumping onto the ends of words. It hopped onto "hop" — and suddenly the word said "hope"! It leapt onto "kit" — "kite!" "I don't make a sound," said little e, "but I make the vowel shout its name!"

activities.prompt: Add e to "pin". What does it say?
Match
In "hope", the e is silent.
Which word has a split digraph?

thinking: Why might English use a silent e instead of a new letter for long sounds?
Can you find a word where the "magic e" rule does not work? (Hint: "have", "give")
speaking: Explain the split digraph to a younger child or a toy using cap and cape.

lessons.title: Read Like a Storyteller
objectives: Use punctuation to read with expression
Retell a short story in order
prerequisites: Reads simple sentences by sounding out
explanation: Fluent readers read smoothly, not word… by… word. They group words into phrases, like "the big red bus", and say them together.
Punctuation is a signal: a full stop means pause; a question mark means your voice goes up; an exclamation mark means say it with feeling!
Good readers also check understanding. After a page, ask: Who is in it? What happened? Why? If something does not make sense, go back and re-read.

vocabulary.meaning: reading smoothly and at a good speed
using your voice to show feeling
marks like . ? ! that guide reading
tell what happened in your own words

examples: "Help!" shouted the cat. — read "Help!" loudly.
"Where is my hat?" — voice goes up at the end.

story.title: The Robot Who Read Too Flat
story.text: Bolt read a story aloud: "THE. WOLF. IS. COMING. RUN." Nobody was scared. Rangi showed Bolt the exclamation mark. Bolt tried again: "The wolf is coming… RUN!" Everyone jumped. "Punctuation tells me how to read," Bolt beeped happily.

activities.prompt: What should your voice do at a question mark?
Match the mark to its job
Put the story in order
Good readers re-read when something does not make sense.

How can the same sentence mean different things if you read it differently?

lessons.title: Build-a-Word
objectives: Use prefixes and suffixes to read and understand longer words
Break multisyllabic words into syllables
explanation: Long words are often built from parts. A root word carries the main meaning: "help". A prefix goes in front and changes meaning: "un-" means not. A suffix goes at the end: "-ful" means full of.
So "unhelpful" = un + help + ful = not full of help. Spotting parts lets you read and understand words you have never seen before.
For other long words, split into syllables — each has one vowel sound: fan-tas-tic, hel-i-cop-ter. Read each chunk, then blend the chunks.

vocabulary.meaning: the main part of a word that carries its meaning
a part added at the start of a word
a part added at the end of a word
a beat of a word with one vowel sound

examples: re + play = replay (play again).
care + less = careless (without care).

story.title: The Word Workshop
story.text: In Tinker Town, Bolt ran a word workshop. A customer wanted a word meaning "not happy". Bolt took the prefix "un-" from the shelf and bolted it onto "happy": "unhappy!" Next someone wanted "full of joy". Bolt fitted "-ful" onto "joy": "joyful!"

Match the prefix to its meaning

lessons.title: Inference Detective
objectives: Make inferences using text clues and background knowledge
Support an inference with evidence from the text
explanation: Authors don't tell us everything. They leave clues. Inference means using those clues plus what you already know to work out what is not said.
Example: "Riya stamped upstairs and slammed her door." The author never says "angry", but stamping and slamming are clues — and we know people do that when they are upset.
Good inference needs evidence. Say: "I think… because the text says…". A guess without a clue from the text is not an inference.

vocabulary.meaning: a conclusion reached from clues and knowledge
words in the text that support an idea
the reason a character does something
exactly what the words say

examples: "He shivered and pulled his scarf tighter" → it is cold.
"Her eyes sparkled as she unwrapped the box" → she is excited or pleased.

story.title: The Muddy Footprints
story.text: Detective Nova found muddy paw prints from the garden to the sofa, a chewed cushion, and a wagging tail sticking out from under a blanket. "Nobody told me who did it," said Nova, "but the clues tell me everything. The puppy has been in the garden — and is very pleased with itself!"

activities.prompt: "Arjun yawned and rubbed his eyes." Arjun is probably…
Which shows an inference with evidence?
options: She is sad because the text says tears ran down her face.

activities.prompt: An inference must be supported by clues in the text.
Match the clue to the inference

Why do authors "show" feelings instead of just telling us?

lessons.title: How Information Is Organised
objectives: Identify common non-fiction text structures
Use structure and features to find and summarise information
prerequisites: Reads fluently and can summarise a paragraph
explanation: Non-fiction writers organise ideas in patterns. Sequence explains steps or time order. Cause and effect explains why something happens. Compare and contrast shows similarities and differences. Problem and solution describes a problem and ways to solve it.
Signal words reveal the structure: "first, then, finally" (sequence); "because, as a result, therefore" (cause–effect); "however, similarly, whereas" (compare); "one solution is" (problem–solution).
Text features help navigation: headings tell you what a section is about, captions explain images, a glossary defines key words, and an index helps you find topics.

vocabulary.meaning: the way information is organised
a word that hints at the structure
a list of key words and meanings
text explaining a picture

examples: "Because forests were cut down, the soil washed away" — cause and effect.
"Frogs have smooth skin, whereas toads have bumpy skin" — compare and contrast.

story.title: Lost in the Library Book
story.text: Zuri needed to find out what tigers eat for a project. She started reading a 200-page book from page one. Nova showed her the index: "Tigers, diet — page 43." Then the heading "What Tigers Eat" and a diagram of a food chain. Zuri found her answer in two minutes.

activities.prompt: Match signal words to structure
A list of key words and their meanings at the back of a book is a…

Headings help readers find information quickly.

thinking: Why might an author choose compare–contrast instead of cause–effect for the same topic?
How can text features sometimes mislead a reader (e.g. a dramatic photo)?
speaking: Explain to someone how you would find one fact in a non-fiction book in under two minutes.

An index is usually at the front of a book.
assessment.why: The contents page is at the front; the index is usually at the back.

Uses features (contents, index, headings, glossary) efficiently
Summarises a non-fiction section accurately

lessons.title: Fact, Opinion and Purpose
objectives: Distinguish facts from opinions in texts
Identify the author's purpose and viewpoint
explanation: A fact can be checked and shown to be true or false: "The Ganga flows into the Bay of Bengal." An opinion is what someone thinks or feels: "The Ganga is the most beautiful river." Opinions can be reasonable or unreasonable, but they cannot be proven true like facts.
Authors write for a purpose: to inform, persuade, entertain or explain. Persuasive texts mix facts with opinions and use emotive words to influence you.
Every author has a viewpoint. Ask: Who wrote this? Why? What did they leave out? Comparing two accounts of the same event reveals different viewpoints.

vocabulary.meaning: a statement that can be checked
a belief or judgement
leaning unfairly to one side
try to make someone agree or act

examples: Advert: "Crunchy-O's — the tastiest cereal ever!" (opinion, persuade).
Encyclopedia: "Cheetahs can reach speeds of over 100 km/h in short bursts." (fact, inform).

story.title: Two Reports of the Match
story.text: After the school football final, two newspapers reported it. The Red Times wrote: "Brilliant Reds deservedly win 2–1!" The Blue Gazette wrote: "Unlucky Blues lose 2–1 after a dubious penalty." Kiko noticed: both agreed on the score — the fact — but told very different stories.

activities.prompt: Which is a FACT?
Match text to purpose
A text can contain both facts and opinions.
Which word signals an opinion?

thinking: Is "Most people in my class like cricket" a fact or an opinion? How could you check?
Why might an author leave out certain facts?
speaking: Find an advertisement and explain to someone which parts are facts and which are opinions, and what it wants you to do.

project.title: Two Sides Newspaper
steps: Pick a simple event (e.g. "the new park opens")
Write a short neutral report with only facts
Rewrite it twice: once strongly for, once strongly against
Highlight opinion words in each version
Present them and explain how viewpoint changes the story

assessment.prompt: "Delhi is the capital of India." This is…
A leaflet saying "Join the best club in town!" mainly wants to…
Opinions can always be proven true.

mastery: Separates fact from opinion with justification
Identifies purpose and viewpoint in varied texts
Compares two accounts and explains differences

lessons.title: Ethos, Pathos, Logos
objectives: Identify the three classical rhetorical appeals
Evaluate whether an argument's evidence and reasoning are sound
prerequisites: Can identify fact, opinion and purpose
explanation: Aristotle described three modes of persuasion: ethos (credibility of the speaker), pathos (appeal to emotion), and logos (appeal to logic and evidence). Most persuasive texts mix all three.
Rhetorical techniques include repetition, rhetorical questions, triads ("tricolon"), and vivid imagery. Recognising them helps you notice when you are being moved — and decide if you should be.

A strong argument has true premises and valid reasoning. Watch for fallacies: attacking the person instead of the argument (ad hominem), misrepresenting an opposing view (straw man), or presenting only two options when more exist (false dilemma).

context.text: The ethos–pathos–logos framework comes from Aristotle's "Rhetoric", written in the 4th century BCE.

vocabulary.meaning: persuasion through credibility
persuasion through emotion
persuasion through logic and evidence
a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument unsound

examples: "As a doctor with 20 years' experience…" — ethos.
"Either we ban all cars or the planet is doomed." — false dilemma.

story.title: The School Debate
story.text: In a debate about longer lunch breaks, Meera said, "Ninety percent of students surveyed reported feeling tired after lunch-rush." Her opponent replied, "Meera just wants to play more football." The judge noted: Meera used logos; her opponent used an ad hominem attack — which didn't answer her evidence at all.

activities.prompt: Match the example to the appeal
"You can't trust his idea about recycling — he failed maths." This is…
An emotional appeal is always a fallacy.
activities.why: Pathos can be legitimate when emotions fit the facts.

activities.prompt: Which is a false dilemma?
options: "You're either with us or against us."

thinking: When is an emotional appeal fair, and when is it manipulative?
Can an argument use a fallacy and still reach a true conclusion?
speaking: Give a one-minute persuasive speech using all three appeals, then ask listeners to identify each one.

Highlight ethos, pathos and logos in three colours

lessons.title: Craft and Theme
objectives: Analyse how specific word choices create effects
Develop and support an interpretation of theme
prerequisites: Can infer and support inferences with evidence
explanation: Close reading means slowing down to notice how a writer creates meaning. Word choice matters: "the house loomed" suggests threat in a way "the house stood" does not. That suggestion is the word's connotation.
Writers shape structure too: who narrates, what is revealed when, and how pacing speeds up or slows down. Foreshadowing plants hints of later events.

A theme is a central idea about life the text explores — not just a topic. "Friendship" is a topic; "true friendship requires honesty even when it hurts" is a theme. Support interpretations with precise evidence and explanation (point–evidence–explain).

vocabulary.meaning: the feelings or ideas a word suggests beyond its literal meaning
hints of what will happen later
a central message or insight about life
language that appeals to the senses

examples: "Her voice was ice" (metaphor) suggests coldness and distance.
Point: the narrator is lonely. Evidence: "the empty chairs stared back". Explain: personifying chairs emphasises her isolation.

story.title: The Same Storm
story.text: Two students described the same storm. One wrote: "It rained heavily." The other wrote: "The sky split open and the rain came down like a punishment." Their teacher asked the class: "What does the second writer want you to feel — and how did they do it in eleven words?"

activities.prompt: "The shadows crept across the floor." The verb "crept" suggests…
A theme is the same thing as the topic of a story.
activities.why: A theme is an insight or message about the topic.

activities.prompt: Order the analysis paragraph
items: Explain: analyse how the evidence supports the claim

activities.prompt: Match the device to the example

thinking: Can a text have a theme the author did not intend? Who decides what a text means?
Why might a writer tell a story from an unreliable narrator's point of view?
speaking: Present a two-minute close reading of a single paragraph from a novel, focusing on three word choices.

project.title: Close Reading Essay
materials: a short story or novel chapter
steps: Choose a passage of about 200 words
Annotate imagery, connotation and structure
Formulate a theme statement
Write a 500-word essay using point–evidence–explain
Revise after reading it aloud

options: War destroys innocence even in those who survive it.

assessment.prompt: A hint early in a story about a later event is…
In close reading, explaining the effect of evidence matters as much as quoting it.
